sections.h2: Where to take a Somerset County deed
sections.html:
Deeds go to the Somerset County Recorder of Deeds, which works from the County Annex Office Building at 300 North Center Avenue, Suite 400, Somerset, PA 15501. The phone number is (814) 445-1547. The courthouse is a separate building at 111 East Union Street, so a seller dropping off paperwork should head to the annex.

The office keeps the county's real property records. More than fifty kinds of documents are filed there, among them deeds, mortgages, easements, powers of attorney, leases, agreements of sale, military discharges, subdivision plans and old mine maps. About 12,000 new documents are recorded each year.

The county's fee schedule was set under Act 45 of 2025. Its minimum covers the state fee and the recording fee for one instrument of up to four pages and four names. Any part of a page counts as a whole page, with no exceptions, so a document that spills a few lines onto a fifth sheet is billed for five.

Somerset County recording checklist
Filing questionAnswer

Charges for additional pages and for each type of document are posted separately by the recorder. Call the office for the current total on your deed before closing, since it depends on page count, names and the kind of instrument.

  • Count pages first, and treat a partial page as a full one.
  • Count every name that has to be indexed.
  • Confirm the fee for any extra document, such as a release or an easement, that comes with the deed.
  • Ask whether the transfer tax is paid separately from the recording fee.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a Somerset County sale
sections.html:
The state levies 1 percent of the transferred value. The recorder collects it, forwards the state's share and handles any local piece owed to the municipality or school district. Some family transfers and property passing under a will or by intestacy are exempt.

If your deed involves a gift, an inheritance or a sale well below market, ask the recorder's staff which transfer tax paperwork applies. The county recorder's web page links to the state's Common Level Ratio information as well. Your sales agreement decides how buyer and seller divide the cost.

Somerset County counts 72,004 residents, a drop of 2.9 percent since 2020, and 38,027 homes and apartments, with owners in 80.4 percent of them. The typical owned home is worth $150,600, and household income at the midpoint is $61,446. About 26.4 percent of residents are 65 or older.

With four in five homes lived in by their owners, many sales involve long-held family houses, and probate paperwork shows up often at the recorder's counter. Somerset borough is the county seat, and other towns include Windber, Meyersdale, Berlin, Boswell, Central City and Confluence. Winters here are real, so buyers look closely at roofs, gutters and heating systems.

The recorder's page offers Landex, an online records service with remote access instructions, plus Record Alert and Notary Alert sign-ups. The office cannot enroll anyone, so register through the Landex links yourself. A Record Alert tells you when anything is filed against your name or property, so a surprise filing does not sit unnoticed.

  • Recorded plat maps are available through the recorder's page.
  • The county GIS parcel viewer draws on Tax Assessment Office and Recorder of Deeds records, but it is not for exact measurement.
  • Plans for wind turbines and towers have their own recording rules, including a minimum sheet size of 18 by 24 inches.

sections.h2: What to prepare before a Somerset County closing
sections.html:
Gather the existing deed, the latest tax bill, any mortgage payoff statement and a legible copy of the survey or plat if you have one. The county parcel viewer helps you check lot lines against the tax map number, and recorded plat maps can be pulled from the recorder's page.

On deed day, count the pages and the names, make sure the notary block is complete, and ask whether your title company will record electronically or in person. A document with a missing acknowledgment costs more time than a lower price ever saves. If a relative died owning the house, the personal representative's authority has to be clear before anyone signs.

sections.h2: Selling a Somerset County house quickly
sections.html:
Recording is the last step, so the sale comes first. A seller in a hurry can consider a direct cash purchase, which avoids showings, repair requests and financing delays. Expect a lower price than a polished listing, and weigh that against the commission and repairs a listing would cost.

Before any closing, pull your deed, get a payoff letter for any mortgage, and ask the recorder's office whether anything recorded against the parcel needs to be released. A paid-off mortgage with no recorded release is the kind of loose end to find before closing day.

Probate comes up often in this county. Before a deed from an estate is signed, the personal representative's authority should be documented, and the title company will want to see it. Transfers under a will or by intestacy can be exempt from the state transfer tax, so ask the recorder's staff which form to file. Keep death-related papers together with the deed, the payoff letter and the tax bill, so nothing has to be hunted down on closing day.

If the house is sold rather than kept in the family, the same recording steps apply. Heirs who live far away can often sign before a notary where they live and send the deed to the title company, which then records it.

• Counting a short last page as no page at all.
  • Leaving a name off the count, so the fee comes up short.
  • Submitting a deed with an incomplete notary block.
  • Forgetting that a release of an old mortgage may need its own filing.

Each of these is cheap to catch on paper and slow to repair after the fact. A quick read-through by your title agent before filing is worth the few minutes it takes.

sections.h2: From signing to a recorded deed
sections.html:
At settlement the deed is signed before a notary. The title company then counts pages and names, calculates the recording fee and transfer tax, and files the deed with the recorder, electronically or in person. The recorder indexes it, and the new owner's name appears in the county records. If a buyer pays cash, the order is the same, but there is no lender to coordinate, so the schedule is shorter.

Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the closing statement with your tax records. If anything looks wrong in the record later, the recorder's office is where a correction starts.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Somerset recorder in person?
faqs.a: The office is at the County Annex Office Building, 300 North Center Avenue, Suite 400, in Somerset. The phone is (814) 445-1547. The courthouse is a separate building at 111 East Union Street.

faqs.q: What does the Somerset minimum recording fee cover?
faqs.a: It covers the state fee and recording fee for one instrument with up to four pages and four names. Call the recorder for the current dollar total for your document.

faqs.q: Is a part of a page billed as a whole page?
faqs.a: Yes. Any fraction of a page is counted as one page, with no exceptions. Check the page count before you submit so the fee is right the first time.

faqs.q: Can I get an alert when a document is recorded on my property?
faqs.a: Yes. The county links to Landex Record Alert and Notary Alert sign-ups. You must register yourself, because the recorder's office cannot sign people up.

faqs.q: Who pays the state transfer tax on a Somerset sale?
faqs.a: Both sides are liable for the 1 percent state tax. Your sales agreement decides how buyer and seller divide the cost.
